creators_or_institution: Multiple institutions; notable frameworks from: University of Sydney (Australia), University of Wyoming, Stanford University, Chartered College of Teaching (UK), University of Western Ontario
background_story: After ChatGPT's release in November 2022, educators rapidly recognized that product-based assessments (submit a final essay, receive a grade) were fundamentally compromised. If a student could generate a polished essay in seconds, the essay itself no longer demonstrated learning. This catalyzed a shift that pedagogical reformers had long advocated: moving to process-based assessment that evaluates how a student arrives at their work, not just what they submit. By 2023, universities across Australia, UK, US, and Canada had begun systematically redesigning assessments to require evidence of process.
how_it_works: Process-based assessment mechanisms: (1) Staged submissions — students submit an outline, annotated bibliography, rough draft, and revised draft at separate deadlines with instructor feedback required between each stage. AI use is detected not by scanning the final product but by the inability to show coherent evolution across stages. (2) Reflective journals — students maintain a learning journal documenting their research process, source evaluation, and thinking changes over time. (3) Portfolio with annotations — students compile work samples with written reflections explaining each piece's significance and their learning process. (4) Version-controlled documents — using Google Docs revision history or GitHub to show actual editing process; rapid production from a blank document is a red flag. (5) Research process documentation — annotated bibliographies with notes on why sources were selected, mind maps, and brainstorming artifacts. The key principle: AI can produce the final product but cannot easily fabricate a convincing, coherent process narrative across multiple interactions.
accuracy_or_effectiveness: Process-based assessment is considered by educational researchers to be more learning-validity-preserving than product-only assessment regardless of AI concerns. For AI detection specifically: it significantly raises the effort required to fraudulently use AI — students must generate an entire fake process, not just a final product. No large-scale studies have measured the exact reduction in AI-assisted cheating from process-based redesign, but qualitative reports from instructors at University of Sydney and University of Wyoming report substantially more evidence of genuine student engagement.
limitations_and_criticisms: Limitations: (1) Significantly increases instructor grading workload — multiple submissions require multiple rounds of feedback. (2) Students can potentially fabricate a fake process (using AI to generate fake drafts with fake 'thinking'). (3) Does not eliminate AI use — students can still use AI as a legitimate learning tool throughout the process (which some policies permit). (4) Logistically challenging at scale — universities with class sizes of 200-500 students face resource constraints for staged feedback. (5) Requires faculty training and buy-in — many faculty resist redesigning long-established assessments.
false_positive_rate: N/A — process-based assessment does not rely on detection tools. False positives are not applicable.
notable_cases_or_examples: University of Sydney: Implemented oral examinations and group projects alongside process portfolios starting 2023; formats designed to reduce AI misuse risk
University of Wyoming: Professor Catherine Hartmann redesigned courses to culminate in individual oral examinations paired with process portfolios
University of Western Ontario and UC San Diego: implemented oral assessments with structured rubrics and trained TAs for courses enrolling hundreds of students

current_status_2024_2026: Process-based and portfolio assessment has become the dominant recommended approach from educational technology experts and faculty development centers as of 2024-2026. Most university teaching centers (Carnegie Mellon, MIT Teaching and Learning Lab, UK Higher Education Academy) now recommend assessment redesign as a primary strategy over AI detection tools. The approach is gaining traction globally, though implementation varies significantly by discipline and institution size.
uncertain: specific percentage reduction in AI-assisted cheating from process-based redesign (no large-scale controlled studies)
